title: The mind is restless
hookLine: after all the instructions, Arjuna says what everyone is thinking, and Krishna agrees with him
carry: practice and letting go: abhyasa and vairagya
last: DIPA — A LAMP OUT OF THE WIND.

cards: You sit down to be still. Ten seconds in, you're thinking about lunch. Then an email.

Then a conversation from 2014 that you lost, and how you should have answered. Then lunch again. Krishna has just described the yogi who sees the self in every being, and the lamp that doesn't flicker.
And Arjuna, a warrior whose whole craft is a steady aim, stops him and says, basically: I can't do this. My mind won't hold still.

teach.b: First, the vision that sets Arjuna off. The yogi, verse twenty-nine says, sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self.

Whoever sees Krishna everywhere and everything in him is never lost to him, and he is never lost to them. And the highest yogi, verse thirty-two, looks at another's joy or pain as if it were their own. Beautiful.
And Arjuna says: this yoga of evenness you describe, I don't see how it can last, because the mind is restless. Verse thirty-four: the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, strong and stubborn.

teach.h: AS HARD AS HOLDING THE WIND.
teach.b: To hold it, I think, is as hard as holding the wind.
Here's the surprise: Krishna doesn't argue. No doubt, he says, the mind is restless and hard to hold. Then he gives two words.
By abhyasa and by vairagya, it can be held.
Abhyasa: practice, doing it again and again. Vairagya: detachment, the fading of the pull, not letting every passing want drag you off. You need both.
Practice alone becomes grim effort against a mind that keeps being yanked away. Detachment alone never builds the habit.
Together they work like two oars. Verse thirty-six closes it: yoga is hard for the one who doesn't hold themselves, but for the one who keeps striving by the right means, it can be reached.
That pair, practice and letting go, became one of the best-known teachings in Hindu spiritual life. The mind is restless. True.
And not the end of the story.

how: Hindu teachers often pair abhyasa (steady practice) and vairagya (detachment) as the two supports of meditation; the Yoga Sutra names the same pair, and some practitioners return to Gita 6.34–35 when meditation feels impossible.

o: forcing the mind to go blank
a song sung at the evening lamp

games.q: what's inside the verses — tap the pairs.
p: as hard to hold as the wind
feels another's pain as their own

s: Krishna tells Arjuna his mind isn't really restless
he agrees: no doubt, the mind is restless and hard to hold.
Arjuna compares holding the mind to holding the wind
verse 34: to hold it is as hard as holding the wind.
the Gita says effort alone will still the mind
it takes two: abhyasa, practice, and vairagya, detachment.

games.q: you're Krishna. Arjuna says his mind is as hard to hold as the wind. what do you say?
o: you're right. by practice and detachment it can be held.
games.why: Krishna agrees first, then answers: abhyasa and vairagya, practice and detachment.

practice: Rest on one thing, the breath at the nose, and come back to it each time the mind runs off, as it will. Notice where it ran; don't chase the thought or argue with it, just let the pull fade a little.
Pull on both oars: return, and let go.

wordCard.voice: Abhyasa. Practice, repeated effort, paired with vairagya, letting go. Arjuna's honest complaint, Gita six, thirty-four: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn. Krishna agrees: by practice and letting go it can be held.

orig.note: Sanskrit: abhyasa, practice, repeated effort; paired in 6.35 with vairagya, detachment.

carryVoice: Carry this: practice and letting go, abhyasa and vairagya. Every wandering is one more stroke of the oar. That's one hundred eighty-one.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 6.33–6.36 (the mind is restless; practice and detachment)
